lead: This unit explains what a fluid is, how its properties are measured, and how fluids at rest press on surfaces. After it you can compute density, viscosity, surface tension, pressure, manometer readings, hydrostatic forces and metacentric height for common exam problems.
about: The unit starts with 1.1, which treats a fluid as a continuum and separates ideal from real fluids. 1.2 defines density, specific weight, specific gravity and compressibility; 1.3 adds viscosity through Newton's law, and 1.4 classifies Newtonian and non-Newtonian behaviour. 1.5 covers surface tension and capillarity. The second half moves to statics: 1.6 gives absolute, gauge and depth-varying pressure; 1.7 uses manometers to measure it; 1.8 turns pressure into forces on plane and curved surfaces; 1.9 applies those forces to buoyancy, floatation and metacentric height. Each chapter uses the earlier definitions, so the numerical problems build from simple property lookups to gate and floating-body stability calculations.

chapters.idea: A fluid is treated as a continuous medium when the length scale of interest is much larger than the distance between molecules.
chapters.depth: Define fluid and continuum; introduce mean free path and the ratio mean free path to body length; ideal fluid has μ = 0 and is taken incompressible, real fluid has viscosity and surface tension. Some syllabi call an ideal fluid inviscid. Keep to definitions and classification only; no flow kinematics.

figure.title: Continuum idea and fluid models
figure.aria: Molecules are averaged into a continuum point, which can be modelled as an ideal fluid with zero viscosity or a real fluid with viscosity.

chapters.example: A pressure sensor has a circular opening of diameter 1 mm. Air at 20 °C and 1 atm has mean free path about 6.8×10⁻⁸ m. Compare the opening with the mean free path. Opening = 1×10⁻³ m; ratio = 1×10⁻³ / 6.8×10⁻⁸ ≈ 1.47×10⁴. Ratio ≫ 1, so the air behaves as a continuum at the sensor scale.
chapters.trap: Calling an ideal fluid one with zero density; ideal means no viscosity, not no mass.
chapters.leave: Eulerian and Lagrangian descriptions, flow classification and continuity to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Density fixes mass per volume, and the other basic properties are simple combinations of density, gravity and pressure change.
chapters.depth: Define ρ = m/V, specific weight γ = ρg, specific gravity SG = ρ/ρ_water, specific volume v = 1/ρ, bulk modulus K = −V dp/dV = ρ dp/dρ and compressibility β = 1/K. Give units and standard values for water, mercury and air. Note that liquids have high K; for a gas, K depends on the process, and isothermal K equals p for an ideal gas.

figure.aria: Density leads to specific weight, specific gravity, bulk modulus and compressibility, with the formula for each shown.

chapters.example: An oil has density 880 kg/m³. Take g = 9.81 m/s² and ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³. (a) Find specific weight and specific gravity. (b) A pressure rise of 2 MPa reduces its volume by 0.1%. Find bulk modulus and compressibility. (a) γ = 880×9.81 = 8632.8 N/m³ ≈ 8.63 kN/m³; SG = 880/1000 = 0.88. (b) ΔV/V = 0.1/100 = 0.001; K = 2×10⁶ / 0.001 = 2×10⁹ Pa = 2 GPa; β = 1/K = 5×10⁻¹⁰ Pa⁻¹.
chapters.trap: Using water density as 1 instead of 1000 kg/m³, or giving specific gravity a unit.
chapters.leave: Pipe friction, flow measurement and compressible flow to Units 3 and 4.

chapters.idea: Viscosity is the fluid property that resists sliding between layers, and Newton's law links shear stress to velocity gradient.
chapters.depth: Define dynamic viscosity μ in Pa·s and kinematic viscosity ν = μ/ρ in m²/s. State Newton's law τ = μ du/dy for parallel layers; explain no-slip at a solid boundary. Mention temperature effect briefly: liquid μ falls as temperature rises, gas μ rises. Do not derive pipe flow.

figure.aria: Shear stress rises in a straight line with velocity gradient; the slope is the dynamic viscosity 0.2 Pa·s.

chapters.example: An oil film of area 0.5 m² lies between a fixed plate and a moving plate. The gap is 1 mm and the moving plate speed is 0.4 m/s. μ = 0.2 Pa·s. Find shear stress and force. du/dy = 0.4/0.001 = 400 s⁻¹; τ = 0.2×400 = 80 Pa; F = τA = 80×0.5 = 40 N.
chapters.trap: Using plate speed instead of velocity gradient, or mixing dynamic viscosity μ with kinematic viscosity ν.
chapters.leave: Laminar pipe flow to Unit 4 and boundary layer ideas to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Newtonian fluids have constant viscosity, while non-Newtonian fluids have shear stress that is not a straight-line function of shear rate.
chapters.depth: Classify Newtonian and non-Newtonian fluids. Cover shear-thinning pseudoplastic, shear-thickening dilatant and Bingham plastic behaviour. Use power law τ = K(du/dy)^n and apparent viscosity μ_app = τ/(du/dy). Name time-dependent thixotropic and rheopectic fluids only. Note that n is not viscosity.

figure.aria: Four flow curves compare a straight Newtonian line, a shear-thinning curve, a shear-thickening curve and a Bingham line with a yield stress.

chapters.example: At shear rate du/dy = 100 s⁻¹ compare four fluids: Newtonian μ = 0.08 Pa·s; pseudoplastic K = 0.5 Pa·s^n, n = 0.6; dilatant K = 0.02 Pa·s^n, n = 1.4; Bingham τ_y = 4 Pa, μ_p = 0.04 Pa·s. Find τ and apparent viscosity μ_app = τ/(du/dy). Newtonian: τ = 0.08×100 = 8 Pa, μ_app = 0.08 Pa·s. Pseudoplastic: τ = 0.5×100^0.6 = 7.92 Pa, μ_app = 0.0792 Pa·s. Dilatant: τ = 0.02×100^1.4 = 12.62 Pa, μ_app = 0.1262 Pa·s. Bingham: τ = 4 + 0.04×100 = 8 Pa, μ_app = 0.08 Pa·s.
chapters.trap: Treating the power-law index n as a viscosity, or forgetting the yield stress in a Bingham plastic.
chapters.leave: Complex rheology and viscoelastic models to later study.

chapters.idea: Surface tension makes a liquid surface behave like a stretched sheet, causing pressure jumps in small drops and capillary rise in narrow tubes.
chapters.depth: Define surface tension σ in N/m. Give pressure difference Δp = 2σ/R for a droplet or a bubble inside a liquid, and Δp = 4σ/R for a soap bubble in air. Define contact angle θ. Derive capillary rise h = 2σ cosθ/(ρgr), with r as tube radius. Explain mercury depression when θ > 90°. Note that σ falls with temperature.

figure.title: Surface tension effects
figure.aria: Surface tension creates a pressure jump in droplets and soap bubbles and drives capillary rise in a narrow tube.

chapters.example: Water rises in a clean glass tube of radius r = 0.5 mm. σ = 0.072 N/m, θ = 0°, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find capillary rise h. h = 2σ cosθ/(ρgr) = 2×0.072×1/(1000×9.81×0.0005) = 0.0294 m = 2.94 cm.
chapters.trap: Using the factor 2 for a soap bubble instead of 4, or using diameter in place of radius.
chapters.leave: Bubble dynamics and two-phase flow are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Pressure is force per area normal to a surface, and in a static fluid it rises linearly with depth.
chapters.depth: Define pressure p = F/A. Give p_abs = p_atm + p_gauge; vacuum is negative gauge pressure. Derive p = p0 + ρgh and pressure head p/(ρg). State that isobars are horizontal in a static fluid of uniform density. Some syllabi add uniform linear acceleration of a liquid container: replace g by an effective gravity; only a few universities ask for full treatment.

figure.aria: Gauge pressure in water increases linearly with depth from 0 to 49.05 kPa at 5 m.

chapters.example: At a point 5 m below the free surface of water, find gauge pressure, absolute pressure and pressure head. p_atm = 101.3 kPa, ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². p_gauge = ρgh = 1000×9.81×5 = 49,050 Pa = 49.05 kPa. p_abs = 101.3 + 49.05 = 150.35 kPa. Pressure head = p_gauge/(ρg) = 5 m of water.
chapters.trap: Adding atmospheric pressure when the question asks for gauge pressure, or measuring depth upward.
chapters.leave: Bernoulli equation and flow measurement to Unit 3; manometer details to Ch 7.

chapters.idea: A manometer measures pressure by balancing it against a column of liquid, using the rule that the same fluid at the same level has the same pressure.
chapters.depth: Cover piezometer, U-tube manometer, differential U-tube, inverted U-tube and inclined manometer. Build the manometer equation by starting at one end: add ρgh when moving down and subtract when moving up. Use gauge pressure at an open end. Mention inclined-tube sensitivity; give one numerical height-difference problem.

figure.title: Manometer equation path
figure.aria: The manometer equation follows the tube from point A down through water, across mercury and up to the open end at atmospheric pressure.

chapters.example: A horizontal pipe carries water. A U-tube mercury manometer is connected. The water column from the pipe centre to the left mercury surface is h1 = 0.40 m. The right mercury surface is h = 0.15 m above the left mercury surface and is open to atmosphere. ρ_water = 1000 kg/m³, ρ_Hg = 13,600 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find gauge pressure in the pipe. Manometer path: p_A + ρw g h1 − ρHg g h = p_atm. p_A − p_atm = ρHg g h − ρw g h1 = 13,600×9.81×0.15 − 1000×9.81×0.40 = 20,012.4 − 3,924 = 16,088.4 Pa ≈ 16.09 kPa.
chapters.trap: Getting plus and minus signs wrong when moving up or down a limb, or using absolute pressure at both ends carelessly.
chapters.leave: Flow meters and orifice problems to Unit 3; forces on gates to Ch 8.

chapters.idea: The pressure distribution on a submerged surface can be replaced by one resultant force acting at the centre of pressure.
chapters.depth: For a plane surface, F = ρg h_c A = p_c A, where h_c is centroid depth. Give y_cp = y_c + I_c/(A y_c), with y measured along the plane from the free surface. For a vertical rectangle with top at the free surface, y_cp = 2h/3. For curved surfaces, horizontal force equals force on the projected vertical area; vertical force equals weight of liquid above the surface. Use pressure prism or pressure volume for line of action.

figure.aria: Hydrostatic force splits into plane-surface and curved-surface methods, with center of pressure and component rules under each.

chapters.example: A vertical rectangular gate is 2 m wide and 3 m high. Its top edge is at the water free surface. Find total hydrostatic force and centre of pressure. ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Area A = 2×3 = 6 m²; centroid depth h_c = 1.5 m. F = ρg h_c A = 1000×9.81×1.5×6 = 88,290 N = 88.29 kN. I_c = bh³/12 = 2×27/12 = 4.5 m⁴. y_cp = y_c + I_c/(A y_c) = 1.5 + 4.5/(6×1.5) = 2.0 m from top.
chapters.trap: Using centroid depth for the centre of pressure, or mixing y along an inclined plane with vertical depth.
chapters.leave: Buoyancy and stability to Ch 9; fluid dynamics to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A body in a fluid feels an upward buoyant force equal to the weight of displaced fluid, and a floating body is stable when its metacentric height is positive.
chapters.depth: State Archimedes principle F_b = ρgV. For a floating body, weight equals buoyancy. Define KB, KG and BM = I/V, where I is the second moment of the waterplane area about the roll axis. Use GM = BM − BG; stable if GM > 0, neutral if GM = 0 and unstable if GM < 0. Small angles only. Mention experimental determination by oscillation period in one line.

figure.title: Floating body stability
figure.aria: Weight and buoyancy act on a floating body; a small tilt gives the metacenter and the sign of GM decides stability.

chapters.example: A rectangular barge is 4 m wide, 10 m long and has mass 20,000 kg. It floats in water. Centre of gravity is 1.0 m above the bottom. ρ = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s². Find draft, BM, GM and state stability. Displaced volume V = mass/ρ = 20 m³. Waterplane area = 4×10 = 40 m²; draft = V/40 = 0.5 m. KB = 0.25 m; KG = 1.0 m; BG = 0.75 m. I = L b³/12 = 10×4³/12 = 53.33 m⁴; BM = I/V = 2.667 m. GM = BM − BG = 1.917 m > 0, stable.
chapters.trap: Using the whole volume of the body instead of displaced volume, or reversing the sign of BG in GM = BM − BG.
chapters.leave: Large-angle stability and ship hydrostatics to later study.
